newsitem.title: FRANCE: French court to rule on Papon, former minister.
newsitem.headline: French court to rule on Papon, former minister.

text.p: After 15 years of procedural battle, a court is to rule on Wednesday whether ex-minister Maurice Papon must stand trial for crimes against humanity for deporting thousands of Jews from wartime France.

Papon, Paris police chief in the 1960s and budget minister in the 1970s before his wartime role was exposed, is accused of deporting 1,690 Jews, including 223 children, in 1942-44 when he was secretary-general of the Bordeaux area administration.
Most were later gassed at the Nazi Auschwitz death camp.

The ruling follows 15 years of procedural wrangling since relatives of the victims started legal action. "After a judicial marathon, we are on the last stretch, the most dangerous as I fear a trick," Gerard Boulanger, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said.
At the hearings in the appeals court of the southwestern town of Bordeaux last March, the public prosecutor recommended that Papon, now 86, face an assize court.
The prosecutor said Papon was responsible for sending Jews onto four trains which left Drancy, near Paris, for the death camps in 1942 and 1944.
Lawyers for relatives of the victims held him responsible for six more trains.
The prosecutor has said Papon must have known about Hitler's "final solution" -- the extermination of the Jews of Europe by the Nazis -- although he had no evidence to back this.
He said Papon, probably the last French official to face such charges, should be tried for complicity to crimes against humanity, arbitrary arrests, kidnappings and persecution.
Papon's lawyer Jean-Marc Varaut has argued that Papon never followed Nazi ideology and had only obeyed orders imposed by the occupying power.
He has said Papon could not be accused of crimes against humanity, the only charge that is not covered by the statute of limitations, and he believed the court would close the case.
Whatever decision is handed down is likely to be appealed by the losing side, again delaying any conclusion to legal action initiated in 1981, legal sources said.
Nazi collaborator Paul Touvier, the only Frenchman sentenced for World War Two crimes against humanity, was jailed for life in 1994. He died in prison last year aged 81.
